report:
**Conclusion: yes—when mask wearing is increased across a community, it can reduce COVID-19 infections, though the size of the effect depends heavily on mask type, fit, adherence, setting, circulating variant, and other measures.**

The strongest direct evidence is a large cluster-randomized trial in 600 rural Bangladeshi villages (342,000 adults). A package that distributed masks and promoted correct public use increased observed masking and reduced *symptomatic, laboratory-confirmed* SARS‑CoV‑2 infections. Effects were clearer for surgical than cloth masks and among older adults. This is particularly relevant to the question because it tested a population-level increase in masking, rather than only asking individuals to mask.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9036942/

Supporting real-world evidence, a study using mask-wearing survey data from regions across six continents estimated that higher population mask use corresponded to a mean 19% reduction in the effective reproduction number (R). Such observational evidence cannot fully exclude confounding—places with greater masking may differ in other protective behaviors—but its direction is consistent with the trial.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9191667/

Important limitation: evidence is not uniformly definitive. The Danish DANMASK-19 randomized trial found no statistically conclusive reduction in infection *for the wearer* from recommending surgical masks, in a setting with uncommon public masking. It did not test widespread masking or primarily measure source control (preventing an infected wearer from infecting others).  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33205991/?dopt=Abstract

Cochrane’s review of randomized evidence found uncertainty and cautioned that trials of interventions intended to promote masking are difficult to interpret; Cochrane subsequently clarified that it should not be read as proving masks “do not work.”  
https://www.cochrane.org/about-us/news/statement-physical-interventions-interrupt-or-reduce-spread-respiratory-viruses-review
